## Stock ownership

A stock is a share of ownership in a company. A public company makes ownership
shares available in public markets and provides required disclosures.
A familiar brand can belong to a private company; popularity alone says nothing
about whether its shares trade publicly or whether its price is attractive.
A ticker identifies a traded security on an exchange. A stock market connects
buyers and sellers. In a new share issue a company can raise money; an ordinary
later exchange trade transfers ownership between investors.

Shareholders can benefit from price increases and dividends, which are cash
distributions when declared. They face price declines, uncertain dividends and
possible loss of the entire amount invested. Ownership is different from lending:
a bond is a debt claim. Public reporting helps research, but does not guarantee
a profitable investment. A company gains access to capital and takes on reporting
costs; investors gain a way to exchange ownership and bear business and market risk.
See the [SEC stock overview](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks).

## Worked paper-portfolio baseline

Use one imaginary $100,000 opening balance. Save the first allocation as the
baseline hypothesis, then keep dated versions of later proposed allocations
in the same workbook. A scenario starts from a named version. The examples
do not add another $100,000 to that workbook.

All C1, C2, C3 and index/fund figures in this course are fictional classroom
data, not prices or results of actual companies. The snapshot is S0; T1 to T4
are the ends of four successive quarters. Cash earns zero; shares allow fractions.
Assume zero dividends, trading costs and taxes in this replay.

| Time | C1 household goods | C2 software | C3 utility | Index X | Index Y | Index Z |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| S0 | $40 | $25 | $50 | 100 | 100 | 100 |
| T1 | $32 | $30 | $51 | 95 | 98 | 90 |
| T2 | $48 | $20 | $52 | 105 | 101 | 112 |
| T3 | $36 | $27.50 | $53 | 100 | 99 | 95 |
| T4 | $60 | $22.50 | $52.50 | 110 | 103 | 118 |

A modeled $20,000 purchase of C1 at $40 buys 500 shares and leaves $80,000 cash.
At T1 the shares are worth $16,000, making the total $96,000. At T4 they are
worth $30,000, making the total $110,000. Portfolio return is
(ending value − opening value) / opening value: 10% over this one-year replay.
The stock's 50% price increase and the whole portfolio's 10% return measure
different exposures. Record quantities, prices, cash and total value separately.
An investment thesis states a reason, evidence, uncertainty and what observation
would cause revision; a profitable replay alone cannot establish a reliable rule.

## Indexes and comparisons

An index summarizes a specified group of securities under a stated weighting rule.
A benchmark is a comparison selected for the question being asked. A portfolio
containing mostly cash and one stock can differ greatly from an all-stock index.
For a price-only return, divide ending price minus opening price by opening price.
A total-return comparison also includes distributions and their reinvestment terms.
Use the same dates, currency, costs and distribution convention for both sides.

## Worked hold versus timing replay

Use INV 1's complete S0–T4 table. Holding 500 C1 shares plus $80,000 cash ends at
$110,000. A fixed alternative sells all 500 at T2 ($48), retains the proceeds,
then reinvests those $24,000 at T3 ($36). Fractional shares are allowed:
24,000 / 36 = 666⅔ shares. At T4 those shares are worth $40,000; total value is
$120,000. If re-entry instead occurs at T4, the final total is $104,000.
This is a comparison of supplied paths. Selecting the best dates after seeing
the table gives hindsight an advantage unavailable when the initial decision
was made. A claim to beat the market needs a predeclared rule and a suitable
benchmark over more than a convenient window.

Index X changes 100 to 110 over S0–T4, a 10% price gain. A separate comparison
allocation of $20,000 to X and $80,000 to cash would end at $102,000. The
baseline C1 portfolio gains 10% while that matching-exposure benchmark gains 2%.
An unscaled comparison with the index's 10% gain would conceal the cash difference.

Bull describes a broadly rising market; bear describes a broadly falling one.
Thresholds and dates matter. A crash is a sharp fall over a short interval;
a long-term trend uses a longer window. These descriptions cannot determine
the next movement. C1 falls from $48 to $36 between T2 and T3, a 25% decline,
while rising over S0–T4. Naming the window makes both observations interpretable.

The fictional X/Y/Z series stand in for comparing differently constructed indexes,
not actual S&P 500, Dow Jones or Nasdaq history. A real-index alternative needs
dated observations and each index's exact name and return convention.

## Growth and purchasing power

Compound growth applies a rate to the entire current balance, including earlier
growth. With starting amount P, constant annual rate r expressed as a decimal
and n whole years, A = P(1 + r)^n when no money is added or withdrawn.
Simple growth instead adds P × r each year. At $100 and 10%, compounding gives
$110 after year one and $121 after year two; simple growth gives $120 at year two.

Inflation means a rise in the general price level. Under a constant 2% annual
inflation assumption, a future amount A has starting-year purchasing power
A / 1.02^n. Thus $121 after two years has purchasing power about $116.30.
A nominal dollar amount and its purchasing power are two views of the same
money, not two balances to add together. Cash held at zero interest loses
purchasing power under positive inflation.

## Worked contributions and timing

Beginning with zero, adding $1,000 at each year-end at a constant 5% model rate
uses next balance = current balance × 1.05 + 1,000.
Year one ends at $1,000; year two at $2,050; year three at $3,152.50.
An initial lump sum, year-start deposits and year-end deposits have different
growth periods. State the sequence before calculating.
[The SEC compound-interest calculator](https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator)
is optional; repeated multiplication and a written table reproduce these cases.

The Rule of 72 estimates doubling years as 72 divided by a positive annual
rate written in percent. At 6%, the estimate is 12 years. Annual multiplication
gives $100 × 1.06^11 ≈ $189.83 and × 1.06^12 ≈ $201.22, so the first whole-year
crossing is year 12. At 10%, 7.2 estimated years falls between whole-year checks:
year seven is about $194.87 and year eight $214.36.
The rule is approximate and assumes continuing positive compound growth.
Zero growth never doubles; a constant negative rate between −100% and 0% shrinks
the balance. At −100% it reaches zero. A past stock-price change supplies no
promise that the same rate will recur. All rates here are hypothetical inputs;
fees, taxes, variable returns and losses can change actual outcomes.

tasks.title: Compounding and Inflation Scenarios
tasks.prompt:
Compare a $100 birthday gift held as zero-interest cash, saved at constant 2%,
and modeled at constant 10% annual compounding. For 1, 5 and 10 years calculate
A = 100(1 + r)^n, then purchasing power A / 1.02^n under constant 2% inflation.
Use no contributions, fees or taxes and round displayed amounts to cents only
after calculating. In a separate model, start at zero at age 25 or 35, deposit
$1,000 at each year-end at constant 5%, and stop at 65: 40 or 30 deposits.
Show contributed totals, ending balances and growth beyond contributions using
the lesson recurrence. Explain the difference between these assumptions and
a forecast. This exercise does not add money to the paper portfolio.

tasks.title: Rule of 72 Portfolio Projection
tasks.prompt:
Compute observed one-year price-only changes for $100→$110, $100→$80 and
$100→$100 using (end − start) / start × 100. Exclude dividends, fees and taxes.
Separately assume constant positive annual rates of 2%, 6% and 10%.
Estimate doubling years with 72 / rate in percent, then repeatedly multiply
$100 by 1 + rate / 100 until the first whole year at or above $200.
Record the preceding balance too. Explain zero and constant negative growth
and why the observed changes do not establish future rates.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Understanding Compounding Returns
tasks.prompt:
Compare $100 at constant 10% for two years under simple and compound
growth. Apply constant 2% inflation to both ending amounts. Explain which
quantity represents growth on earlier growth.

tasks.title: Extension Review: Understanding Compounding Returns
tasks.prompt:
Compare three $1,000 deposits made at year-end versus year-start over
three years, both starting at zero with constant 5% annual growth.
Write the update order and ending amount for each. Explain why the difference
does not represent an extra contribution.

## Risk and return

Risk includes uncertainty about outcomes and possible loss. Return measures gain
or loss relative to the amount exposed. Volatility measures variation in returns;
it does not capture every risk, such as needing cash before an asset can be sold.
Risk tolerance describes willingness to accept uncertainty; risk capacity concerns
the ability to absorb loss given goals and obligations. A short time horizon can
make a volatile allocation unsuitable for a supplied goal even when its owner
is comfortable with risk.

## Worked equal-average comparison

In the dice model independent rolls of a fair six-sided die have probability 1/6 for each face.
Pay $1 before each round, select g distinct faces, receive $6/g including the
stake on a match, or zero on a miss. The possible net results are 6/g − 1
and −1. Their weighted average is
(g/6)(6/g − 1) + (1 − g/6)(−1) = 0.
For g = 6 every round nets zero; for g = 1 a round gains $5 or loses $1.
Equal expected net results therefore do not mean equal uncertainty.
A short replay can finish above or below its expectation.

## Optional Sharpe calculation

For a backward-looking comparison, subtract a benchmark return from each
portfolio return in the same period and units. The historical Sharpe ratio
is the mean of these differential returns divided by their standard deviation.
Use sample standard deviation here: subtract the mean, square the differences,
sum them, divide by n − 1, then take the square root. At least two observations
and a nonzero standard deviation are needed for this calculation.
[Sharpe's original explanation](https://web.stanford.edu/~wfsharpe/art/sr/sr.htm)
describes the historical ratio and its limitations.

For quarterly portfolio returns 2%, −1%, 3%, 0% and a constant quarterly
benchmark of 0.25%, differentials are 1.75%, −1.25%, 2.75%, −0.25%.
Their mean is 0.75 percentage points. Squared deviations from that mean sum
to 10 squared percentage points; sample deviation is √(10/3) ≈ 1.8257
percentage points. The quarterly ratio is 0.75 / 1.8257 ≈ 0.4108.
There is no annualization in this exercise. A benchmark called risk-free in a
model is an assumption for that period; choosing it does not remove portfolio
risk. The ratio summarizes this sample and cannot guarantee future results.

tasks.title: Dice Risk Ledger
tasks.prompt:
Start each of three separate replays with $20. Pay $1 before every round.
With g distinct guessed faces, a match pays $6/g including the stake;
a miss pays $0. Payouts for g = 1/2/3/4/5/6 are $6/$3/$2/$1.50/$1.20/$1.
For g = 1, 3 and 6 always select faces 1 through g, then use rolls
2, 5, 1, 6, 3. Record opening balance, cost, match, payout and closing balance
for all five rounds. Compare the possible net round outcomes, expected net
result and actual replay result. Explain why a replay cannot predict a portfolio.

tasks.title: Sharpe Ratio Portfolio Review
tasks.prompt:
Use quarterly returns 2%, −1%, 3%, 0% and constant quarterly benchmark 0.25%.
Calculate differential returns, their mean and sample standard deviation
(divide squared-deviation sum by 3), then the unannualized historical Sharpe
ratio. Use identical percent units throughout. Repeat conceptually for four
identical differential returns of 1% and explain why the ordinary ratio is
undefined. State one risk the ratio leaves out and one limitation of four quarters.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Assessing My Portfolio's Risk
tasks.prompt:
For g = 2 in the lesson dice model, write match probability, net gain on a
match, net loss on a miss and expected net per round. Explain why five consecutive
misses remain possible even though expected net is zero.

tasks.title: Extension Review: Assessing My Portfolio's Risk
tasks.prompt:
Two fictional goals each have $2,000: A needs the full amount for a fixed
bill next month; B is a discretionary purchase ten years away.
A supplied risky scenario can reduce either balance by 30%; a cash scenario
earns zero with immediate access. Calculate the risky ending amount and each
goal's shortfall relative to $2,000. Explain how timing and flexibility affect
capacity without declaring one risk tolerance for every person.

## Bonds and funds

A bond is a loan to an issuer. Face value is the amount scheduled for repayment
at maturity; a coupon is a contractual interest payment, subject to the issuer's
ability to pay. A fictional $1,000 face-value, three-year bond with a 4% annual
coupon pays $40 at each year-end, with $1,000 principal also due at year three.
Total scheduled receipts are $1,120. A $40 coupon is 4% of face value; it is not
automatically the return of someone buying the bond at a different market price.
When market interest rates rise, an existing fixed-rate bond generally becomes
less attractive and its market price can fall. Default, inflation and selling
before maturity create additional uncertainty.
See [bond basics](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds).

A fund pools investors' money to hold assets. An ETF is a fund whose shares
trade on an exchange. An index fund follows an index strategy; ETF describes a
vehicle and index describes a strategy. A specialized ETF can concentrate in
one sector. A bond fund holds bonds but its share price can change; owning its
shares is different from receiving one individual bond's scheduled principal.
Liquidity concerns access to a sale and its price, not a guarantee against loss.
See the [SEC fund overview](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/mutual-funds-and-exchange-traded-2).

## Worked fund comparison

| Fund | Holdings | S0 share price | Annual expense ratio |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| B | 40% C1, 30% C2, 30% C3 | $50 | 0.20% |
| T | 100% C2 | $25 | 0.60% |
| G | Fictional fixed-rate bond pool | $100 | 0.30% |

B is a three-company teaching index fund, not a broad market in itself.
T adds the same company exposure as buying C2 directly.
At a constant $20,000 average balance, 0.20% represents about $40 annual
fund expenses. Actual expenses depend on the fund's method and assets.
A return explicitly stated as net of expenses already includes that deduction.

For a proposal using the same $100,000 opening balance, $40,000 in B buys
800 shares, $30,000 in G buys 300, and $30,000 remains cash.
Under a separate one-year scenario with B +8%, G +2% and cash 0%, all net
of fund expenses, ending value is $43,200 + $30,600 + $30,000 = $103,800.
Do not subtract the expense ratios again. This scenario is independent of
INV 1's quarter-price replay; it is a planning comparison, not an observed result.

## Underlying exposure and concentration

Diversification spreads exposure among assets whose outcomes can differ.
Concentration means much of the result depends on one company, sector or other
shared risk. Owning many fund names can still concentrate in the same holdings.
Look through each fund: amount in a company = direct amount + fund amount
multiplied by that company's fund weight. Portfolio weights sum to 100%.

## Worked underlying exposure

Use the fictional INV 5 fund sheet. Proposal A holds 40% C2, 40% T and 20% cash.
Because T holds only C2, total C2 exposure is 80%.
Proposal B holds 20% C2, 40% B, 20% G and 20% cash.
B contributes 16% C1, 12% C2 and 12% C3, so total exposures are
16% C1, 32% C2, 12% C3, 20% bonds and 20% cash.
For these instantaneous shock comparisons ignore fund expenses and hold
fund weights fixed. With hypothetical company returns C1 −10%, C2 −20%, C3 +5% and bonds/cash 0%,
A changes by 80% × −20% = −16%. B changes by
16% × −10% + 32% × −20% + 12% × 5% = −7.4%.
In a different shock with only C3 −50%, A is unchanged and B loses 6%.
Diversification changes exposure; it cannot assure a gain or outperform in
every scenario. The [SEC allocation overview](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation)
connects this principle to goals and risk.

Cyclical businesses are sensitive to economic activity; defensive businesses
sell goods/services with comparatively steady demand. Growth describes expected
business expansion, not a guaranteed share return. Blue-chip is an informal
description of an established major company, not a safety certification.
An IPO is an initial public offering, an event rather than a permanent sector.
These categories overlap. A large software company can be established, growth
oriented and economically sensitive at the same time.

Sector rotation changes industry allocations as conditions or expectations change.
The optional exercise compares supplied historical-style fictional snapshots;
it does not teach that a cycle label predicts future winners.

proposal with amounts and quantities at S0; preserve earlier workbook versions.

reading:
## Business results and price

Revenue is the amount earned from sales during a period; expenses are costs
recognized for that period. Net income is revenue minus all applicable
expenses. An income statement reports these flows over time; a balance sheet
reports assets and liabilities at one date; a cash-flow statement explains
cash movements. Profit can differ from cash received because the timing and
recognition rules differ. Read the period, currency and units before comparing.
The [SEC financial-statement guide](https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/investorpubsbegfinstmtguide)
explains these distinctions.

## Worked matched annual statements

Each cell below is revenue / total expenses in millions of dollars. Assume
no preferred shares and constant common-share counts for this simplified EPS.
FY-A, FY-B and FY-C are consecutive complete years, all ending before S0.

| Company | FY-A | FY-B | FY-C | Common shares, millions | S0 price |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C1 | 100 / 85 | 110 / 94 | 120 / 102 | 10 | $40 |
| C2 | 80 / 75 | 120 / 110 | 150 / 145 | 10 | $25 |
| C3 | 150 / 135 | 154 / 139 | 160 / 144 | 20 | $50 |

C1's net incomes are $15m, $16m and $18m. Latest margin is 18/120 = 15%.

Simplified earnings per share (EPS) are net income divided by common shares:
$18m/10m = $1.80. Trailing price/earnings (P/E) compares S0 price with latest
complete-year EPS: 40/1.80 ≈22.22. Use one consistent reporting window and
distinguish trailing earnings from forecasts.

C2 grows revenue from $80m to $150m while latest net income returns to $5m;
more sales alone do not establish improving profit.
A company with negative or zero EPS has no meaningful positive P/E comparison
under this method. A negative arithmetic quotient is unsuitable for ranking alongside positive
multiples as evidence of a cheap business.

Undervaluation is a thesis that price is low relative to a reasoned estimate
of value. A low P/E alone does not prove it: falling earnings, debt, poor cash
generation or different growth expectations can explain different multiples.
A usable thesis states supporting facts, contrary evidence, missing information
and a condition for revision. A strong business and an attractive purchase
price are separate questions.

Private-company information may be limited, and shares may be difficult to sell.
A research ranking needs customer demand, differentiation, team capability,
business economics, mission and runway: months before cash is exhausted under
a stated spending model. A ranking of supplied cases is not an instruction
to invest or evidence that an offering is accessible.

tasks.title: Financial Statement and P/E Ratio Review
tasks.prompt:
Use INV 7's matched FY-A/B/C statements and S0 prices. For each company compute
three annual net incomes, latest net margin, latest EPS and trailing P/E.
Compare C1 and C2's sales/profit trends, then explain whether their multiples
alone establish a better purchase. Keep millions consistent in EPS calculations.
For the original optional research alternative, compare Tesla with GM using
dated issuer filings for matched complete periods and one common price date.
The supplied C1/C2 figures are not Tesla or GM results.

tasks.title: Undervalued Stock Candidate Review
tasks.prompt:
Compare C1/C2/C3 using the supplied INV 7 table, with all values measured at S0.
Choose one or two candidates for further research, calculate their latest P/E
and state a provisional value thesis with one contrary fact and one missing
fact. A fourth fictional company D has FY-C net loss $2m, 4m common shares and
S0 price $10. Explain how D changes a simple 'lowest P/E wins' ranking.
Record a hold/research/revise decision for the paper portfolio, with a reason.

tasks.title: Private Company Ranking Case
tasks.prompt:
Use three fictional snapshots; figures are claims awaiting verification.
A: repairable household sensor, two experienced engineers, 18 paid trials with
12 repeat users, 8 months runway, mission reducing waste.
B: crowded delivery app, three experienced operators, 60 trials with 40 repeat
users, 3 months runway, mission improving delivery access.
C: novel water filter, one first-time founder, 4 unpaid pilots and 0 repeat
orders yet, 12 months runway, mission cleaner water.
Rank all three with five equally weighted criteria: differentiation, team,
product/demand, mission evidence and survival/runway. Give each 0–2
(0=missing/weak evidence,1=mixed,2=stronger supplied evidence), state the reason,
and test a ranking with runway weighted twice. Different trial populations
and product-use cycles limit direct comparisons. Public [Republic.co](https://republic.co/) research
is an optional substitute with dated sources; no account is needed.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Assessing a Company's Success
tasks.prompt:
A fictional income statement reports $200m revenue and $184m total
expenses, with 8m common shares and price $30. Calculate net income, margin,
EPS and trailing P/E. Identify the error in dividing $16m by the number 8
and calling the answer dollars per share.

tasks.title: Extension Review: Assessing a Company's Success
tasks.prompt:

reading:
## ESG evidence

Environmental criteria concern effects such as energy, waste and emissions.
Social criteria concern relationships with employees, customers, communities
and suppliers. Governance concerns how a company is directed and held accountable,
including oversight, reporting and shareholder rights.
A policy states an intention; a measured outcome needs a definition, date,
boundary and evidence. 'We will reduce emissions' differs from a verified
year-to-year change measured on the same basis.

Scores combine selected observations using a method. Check scale direction,
weights, missing data, industry comparisons, dates and conflicts of interest.
Two providers may ask different questions and disagree without either number
being a universal ethical verdict.
The [SEC ESG bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/environmental-social-and-governance-esg-funds-investor-bulletin)
describes differences among approaches and ratings.

## Worked fictional methods

Higher is better on every supplied 0–100 scale. C1 has E90/S40/G60;
C2 has E50/S80/G90. Method M uses .7E + .3S; method N uses .3E + .7S.
M gives C1 75 and C2 59; N gives C1 55 and C2 71.
The ranking reverses solely because weights change. Both methods omit governance;
neither result is a complete assessment or an actual company's score.

For a simple evidence check, C1 reports 100 tonnes of emissions in year A
and 80 in year B under the same boundary, with independent measurement supplied
for this case. That is a 20% reduction. If its output fell from 100 to 50 units,
emissions per unit increased from 1 to 1.6 tonnes, a 60% rise. Absolute and
intensity measures answer different questions.
A values-based allocation must specify its criterion, evidence standard and
tradeoffs with concentration, financial risk and missing data. A high score
does not establish an attractive price or future return.

tasks.title: ESG Criteria and Reliability Review
tasks.prompt:
Use the fictional C1/C2 E/S/G scores and both methods in INV 8. Calculate the
four composite scores, rank each method and identify an omitted category.
Then compare C1's absolute emissions with emissions intensity using the supplied
100→80 tonnes and 100→50 output units. Write a claim that both measures support
without hiding either result. An optional Alphabet, Disney, and PepsiCo comparison
uses dated company evidence and named rating methods; the classroom scores
are not actual ratings for those companies.

tasks.title: Values-Aligned Portfolio Update
tasks.prompt:
Use the supplied scores for C1/C2 in INV 8. For C3 use E70/S70/G80.
Compare two classroom criteria: (A) E at least70 and G at least70;
(B) equal-weight mean E/S/G at least70. Calculate eligibility under each.
From one existing portfolio version, propose a new $100,000 allocation using
eligible companies and/or cash; sum it and identify concentration and missing
impact evidence. If retaining B, look through its C1/C2/C3 holdings before
claiming all holdings meet a screen. Record an alternative decision under
the other criterion. No single values choice is prescribed.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Holding Companies Socially Responsible
tasks.prompt:

'We aim to halve waste by year5'; 'a verified meter measured80 tonnes in yearB';
'the board has three independent members out of five'; 'our product is ethical'.
Explain why a policy and a measured result need distinct labels.

tasks.title: Extension Review: Holding Companies Socially Responsible
tasks.prompt:

and S weight1−w, omitting G. Solve the equality point, then evaluate w=.25

## Borrowed shares and loss risk

A short sale begins by borrowing shares, selling them, later buying shares to
return to the lender, and settling borrowing obligations. A lower repurchase
price can produce a gain; a higher price produces a loss. Sale proceeds are
accompanied by the obligation to return shares, not unrestricted new wealth.
This lesson is paper analysis of the mechanism.
The [SEC short-sale bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-51)
describes borrowing, fees and loss risk.

## Worked short ledger

In a deliberately simplified model, borrow and sell 10 shares at $50, receiving
$500. Assume a fixed $5 total borrowing/transaction charge, no dividends,
no tax and no other charges. Cover means buy shares to return.
Covering at $30 costs $300 and leaves profit $500 − $300 − $5 = $195.
Covering at $80 costs $800 and creates loss $500 − $800 − $5 = −$305.
A long purchase of the same shares for $500 can lose its $500 purchase cost;
a short position's repurchase price has no finite upper bound in this model.
A planned exit price alone cannot establish a hard maximum loss.

A short squeeze is a price rise that pressures short sellers to buy shares to
cover, potentially adding demand and further upward pressure. Other buying,
limited liquidity and other market conditions can also influence prices.
In a supplied fictional sequence $50→$65→$80, the short's cost to cover rises
from $500 to $650 to $800. A correct concern about business fundamentals does
not ensure that a short position survives a price rise.

For a separate exit scenario, the plan says 'review/cover at $55', but the next
available simulated execution is $80. The modeled loss remains $305.
This case assumes that fill price; it does not promise a particular market
order execution or teach operational trading. A hypothetical loss budget must
be tested against gaps, fees and inability to close at the preferred price.

## Jordans resale analogy

For a fictional borrowing agreement, receive one specified pair of Jordans,
sell it for $200, then buy an equivalent pair to return by the agreed date.
Ignore charges and assume the agreement permits this resale and replacement.
At a $150 replacement price the net result is +$50; at $300 it is −$100.
The obligation remains after the first sale. Real shoes can differ in condition,
size and availability; the analogy illustrates the return obligation, not
identical market mechanics.

## GameStop historical case

The [SEC staff report on early 2021 markets](https://www.sec.gov/files/staff-report-equity-options-market-struction-conditions-early-2021.pdf),
section 3.4 and Figure 6, examines January 2021 GameStop trading.
Staff observed buying by short-covering participants during some sharp price
increases, while attributing the sustained multiweek rise to broader positive
sentiment rather than covering alone. A covering mechanism and an explanation
of the entire event are different claims. This summary supplies the historical
context for the local ledger; its $50/$65/$80 path is fictional, not GameStop data.

tasks.title: Short Selling and Short Squeeze Case
tasks.prompt:
Use the lesson's 10-share $50 short with fixed $5 total charge and no dividends,
taxes or other costs. Draw the borrow/sell/buy/return sequence. Compute cash
received, cost to cover and net result at $30, $65 and $80. Explain why receiving
$500 on sale does not create $500 of net wealth. In the supplied $50→$65→$80
sequence, describe how covering could add buying pressure and name another
possible reason for rising prices. Keep the case separate from the long-only
paper-portfolio allocation; it is a counterfactual risk exercise.

Apply the lesson's Jordans resale analogy at $150 and $300 replacement
prices. Then explain, using the supplied GameStop report summary, why evidence
of some covering does not establish that covering caused the entire rise.

tasks.title: Overvalued Company Short Plan
tasks.prompt:

Choose one as a provisional overvaluation research hypothesis, stating missing
evidence. For a separate modeled position, short10 shares of a candidate at
$50 with a fixed $5 charge. A plan targets $30, reviews at $55 and budgets $60
of loss. Compute results at cover prices $30,$55 and a supplied gap execution
of $80. Decide whether the claimed $60 cap holds. A defensible final plan may
reject the position; a price target is not a guaranteed future execution.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Shorting Stocks
tasks.prompt:

tasks.title: Extension Review: Shorting Stocks
tasks.prompt:

## Money and transaction networks

Fiat currency is government-issued money whose value is not a promise to redeem
a fixed quantity of a commodity. Acceptance, institutions, supply and demand
affect its purchasing power. Cryptocurrency uses cryptography and a network's
rules to record and transfer units. A blockchain groups records into linked
blocks; participating computers maintain and check a ledger. A private key
can authorize transfers, so loss or theft of access is a separate risk from
price fluctuation. Custody means responsibility for that access.

[Bitcoin's explanation](https://bitcoin.org/en/how-it-works) describes a shared
transaction ledger and peer-to-peer transfers.
[Ethereum](https://ethereum.org/what-is-ethereum/) supports programmable
applications as well as transfers; ether is its native cryptocurrency.
[Dogecoin](https://dogecoin.com/dogepedia/articles/what-is-dogecoin/) is a
peer-to-peer cryptocurrency with a public ledger.
A technical purpose and a community's enthusiasm do not establish a fair price.
Network rules, issuance and control differ across assets; 'decentralized' needs
a specific question about who validates, controls changes or holds the units.
Currency use, speculative demand, fees, access, custody and volatility can
produce different benefits and risks.
The [SEC crypto overview](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/crypto-asset-related-investments)
provides additional risk context.

## Worked valuation and price path

Coin R has price $2 and circulating supply1,000: circulating market capitalization
is $2,000. Coin S has price $50 and circulating supply20: capitalization is $1,000.
A lower unit price does not make R smaller or demonstrate a bargain.
Market capitalization is price × a stated supply measure, not a cash reserve
available to holders. Circulating, total and maximum supply are different inputs.

For a separate fictional path, prices at dates A/B/C/D are $.25/$10/$2/$4.
A $100 purchase at A buys400 units and ends D at $1,600 (+1,500%).
At B it buys10 units and ends at $40 (−60%); at C it buys50 and ends at $200 (+100%).
Assume fractional units allowed, no interest, fees or tax, and unchanged units held.
The path is not Bitcoin history and its early low price is not a generally
available opportunity. Entry dates, access, costs and losses matter to any
historical comparison. The lesson uses supplied data; wallet setup and purchases
are outside its completion requirements.

tasks.title: Cryptocurrency Value Comparison
tasks.prompt:
Use INV 10's descriptions of fiat money, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Dogecoin to
compare issuer/network, transfer record, possible purpose and one unresolved
risk. Distinguish a network's purpose from evidence of price value.
Calculate circulating capitalization for fictional R($2,1,000units) and
S($50,20units). In a separate algebra scenario, R's supply doubles to2,000
while its total capitalization is held fixed at $2,000. Calculate implied
unit price and explain why that assumption is not a prediction.
Optional public Bitcoin/Ether/Dogecoin directory research must label every
price/supply observation with source, date and supply definition.

tasks.title: Bitcoin Historical Return Case
tasks.prompt:
For a complete local calculation, use the explicitly fictional INV 10 price
path A/B/C/D=$.25/$10/$2/$4. Compare three separate $100 purchases at A,B,C
held to D with no fees,taxes,interest or new units. Compute units, ending
value and percentage gain/loss, and explain entry-date selection bias.
These figures are not actual Bitcoin prices or 2018 observations.
For the original historical alternative, use a public
[Bitcoin price chart](https://www.coindesk.com/price/bitcoin), name exact early,
2018 peak, post-crash and terminal dates, and retain same-currency price
observations and source dates. If that evidence is unavailable, submit the
supplied path with its fictional label and state the historical limitation.

tasks.title: Practice Map: Understanding the Value of Cryptocurrency
tasks.prompt:

Compute both percentage changes and the overall $10→$4 change.
Explain why adding the two percentages gives the wrong overall result.

tasks.title: Extension Review: Understanding the Value of Cryptocurrency

to zero-interest cash. Scenario1:R−80%; scenario2:R+100%.

## Portfolio reasoning

An analytical strategy brief makes a portfolio proposal reproducible.
State its opening snapshot, goal and time horizon; list dollar amounts,
prices, quantities and cash; total the weights; then look through funds
for repeated holdings. Connect evidence to each choice and state uncertainty
and conditions that would change it. A private written brief or presentation can use the same evidence record.

## Worked capstone version

Use the fictional S0 prices from INV 1/5, the same $100,000 opening balance,
zero trading costs/taxes and these proposed allocations:

| Holding | Dollars | S0 price | Quantity | Opening weight |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C1 | $10,000 | $40 | 250 | 10% |
| C2 | $10,000 | $25 | 400 | 10% |
| C3 | $10,000 | $50 | 200 | 10% |
| B | $30,000 | $50 | 600 | 30% |
| G | $30,000 | $100 | 300 | 30% |
| Cash | $10,000 | — | — | 10% |

Underlying exposure is C1 22%, C2 19%, C3 19%, bonds30%,cash10%.
The case's classroom limits are each company at most25%, each stock sector
at most35%, cash at least10% and optional crypto at most5%, all measured at
the opening snapshot. These are exercise constraints, not universal advice.

Use a one-year scenario separate from the earlier price replay. In scenario U,
each direct stock returns+10%, B's gross basket return is+10%, G's gross
return is+2%, and cash earns0%. For this simplified fee model, deduct fund
expenses once at year-end as .20% of B's opening balance and .30% of G's
opening balance. B's net return is+9.8%, G's+1.7%; ending value is $106,450.
In scenario D, each direct stock and B's gross basket return−20%, G's gross
return−5%, and cash0%. After the same opening-balance expense charges,
B's net return is−20.2%, G's−5.3%; ending value is $86,350. State both results. An allocation must
not be described as loss-proof because it passes an opening limit.
The classroom opening-balance expense charge is .002×30,000 + .003×30,000=$150;
do not subtract it again from these net scenario results.

A review rule names a cadence and a trigger. This example reviews quarterly,
checks underlying weights against the supplied limits, and records the reason
for holding or rebalancing. Rebalancing restores chosen weights by changing
positions; it can create costs and does not predict the market.
A projection states assumptions and scenarios; expected return requires
additional assumptions about probabilities. Without probabilities, a midpoint
of U and D is merely a midpoint, not an established expectation.

The final brief retains the baseline and a change log, sources/dates for real
research, model labels for fictional data, evidence of loss risk and a
monitoring rule. It evaluates the proposal; public promotion and real
transactions are outside this course's completion requirements.

tasks.title: Investment Strategy Pitch

a balanced $100,000 allocation and its changed exposure. Present a private
analytical brief with goal, horizon, evidence, contrary evidence, uncertainty,
quarterly review trigger and a change log from the INV 1 baseline.
No actual return probability or future market return is supplied.
